subject: Vocabulary
description: High-hit one-word-for-a-phrase questions in SSC / Bank papers

questions.stem: One who does not believe in the existence of God:
questions.explanation: Atheist — denies God's existence. Agnostic — neither believes nor disbelieves; considers it unknown. Theist — believes in God. Heretic — one who opposes established religious dogma (regardless of God-belief).
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.explanation: BIBLIO (book) + PHILE (lover). Philanthropist — lover of humankind. Philatelist — stamp collector. Numismatist — coin / currency collector.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.explanation: Extempore / impromptu — off-the-cuff speech. Eulogy — speech of praise (often at a funeral). Manifesto — written declaration of aims (esp. political). Sermon — religious discourse.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: One who studies or works with insects:
questions.explanation: Near-twin trap. Entomology (entomon = insect) — insects. Etymology — origin of words. Ornithology — birds. Ichthyology — fish. Herpetology — reptiles. Mammalogy — mammals.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: An animal that feeds on FLESH:
questions.explanation: Carnivore (Latin carnis = flesh). Herbivore — plants. Omnivore — both. Frugivore — fruits. Insectivore — insects. Piscivore — fish.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.explanation: Orphanage — home for orphans. Hostel — accommodation (students etc.). Asylum — refuge, esp. for the mentally-ill historically, or for refugees (political asylum). Sanatorium — a medical establishment for long-term illness, esp. TB.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.explanation: OLIGO (few) + -ARCHY (rule). Democracy — by the people. Monarchy — one ruler (king/queen). Theocracy — rule by religious authority. Plutocracy — rule by the wealthy. Meritocracy — rule by the able.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Something that CANNOT be corrected / amended:
questions.explanation: Irrevocable — not able to be called back or changed. Inevitable — certain to happen. Irrelevant — not pertinent. Ineffable — too great to be expressed in words. Near-twin trap!
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Which one-word substitution best describes a creature that feeds on both plant matter and animal flesh?

options.option_text: Omnivore — one who consumes both plant-based and animal food
Herbivore — one who feeds exclusively on plant-based material
Carnivore — one who feeds exclusively on the flesh of animals
Insectivore — one who feeds primarily on insects and small bugs

questions.explanation: A is correct: 'Omnivore' derives from Latin omni (all) + vorare (to eat), meaning one that eats both plants and animals. Carnivore is a common wrong pick because it sounds similar but refers strictly to flesh-eaters; herbivore and insectivore are narrower diet categories that do not include both kingdoms.

questions.stem: A system of governance in which religious leaders or priests rule as direct representatives of God is called?

options.option_text: Democracy — a government chosen by the votes of ordinary citizens
Plutocracy — a government controlled by the wealthiest social class
Theocracy — a government ruled directly by religious clergy or priests
Bureaucracy — a government administered by unelected official departments

questions.explanation: C is correct: 'Theocracy' comes from Greek theos (God) + kratos (rule), denoting governance in the name of a deity. Plutocracy is a tempting distractor because it also ends in '-cracy', but it specifically means rule by the wealthy, not by religious authority.

questions.stem: A person who habitually walks or performs physical actions while remaining in a deep state of sleep is called?

options.option_text: Insomniac — a person who chronically cannot fall or stay asleep
Somnambulist — a person who walks and acts during periods of deep sleep
Narcoleptic — a person who experiences sudden and uncontrollable sleep attacks
Somniloquist — a person who speaks aloud during episodes of deep sleep

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'Somnambulist' comes from Latin somnus (sleep) + ambulare (to walk), precisely describing sleepwalking behaviour. Somniloquist is the most dangerous distractor — it shares the root somnus and also refers to sleep behaviour, but specifically means talking in sleep, not walking.

questions.stem: The art of producing visually beautiful and decorative handwriting using a pen, brush, or quill is known as?

options.option_text: Typography — the art of arranging and styling printed typefaces on a page
Stenography — the art of writing in rapid shorthand symbols for speed
Calligraphy — the art of fine decorative penmanship and ornate lettering
Lithography — the art of printing from a flat stone or prepared metal plate

questions.explanation: C is correct: 'Calligraphy' derives from Greek kallos (beauty) + graphe (writing), meaning aesthetically beautiful handwriting. Typography is the strongest distractor because it also concerns letterforms, but it refers to arranging pre-made typefaces in print, not the manual art of beautiful script.

questions.stem: A person whose guiding philosophy holds that the active pursuit of personal pleasure is the highest purpose of life is called?

options.option_text: Stoic — one who suppresses desires and endures hardship with indifference
Epicurean — one who seeks refined and sophisticated sensory enjoyment daily
Altruist — one who selflessly prioritises the welfare and needs of others
Hedonist — one who holds pleasure-seeking as the supreme goal of existence

questions.explanation: D is correct: 'Hedonist' (Greek hedone = pleasure) specifically identifies someone for whom pleasure is the ultimate moral good and life-goal. Epicurean is the trap — it also involves pleasure but refers narrowly to the refined enjoyment of food, art, and comfort; Epicurus himself advocated modest pleasures, not pleasure as the sole purpose.

questions.stem: A scholar whose professional vocation is to compile, write, edit, and define words in a dictionary is known as?

options.option_text: Etymologist — one who traces the historical origins and evolution of words
Philologist — one who studies language through its ancient texts and manuscripts
Lexicographer — one who compiles and edits dictionaries as a formal profession
Grammarian — one who systematically studies and codifies the rules of language

questions.explanation: C is correct: 'Lexicographer' comes from Greek lexikon (of words) + graphein (to write), and is the precise term for a dictionary compiler or editor. Etymologist is the primary distractor because it also deals with words, but its focus is exclusively on tracing word origins and derivations, not on compiling a comprehensive reference work.

questions.stem: A marital custom or social institution in which one woman simultaneously has more than one husband is specifically called?

options.option_text: Polygamy — the practice of one person having several spouses of any gender
Polyandry — the practice of a woman being married to several men at once
Polygyny — the practice of a man simultaneously maintaining multiple wives
Bigamy — the criminal act of contracting a marriage while still legally wed

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'Polyandry' derives from Greek poly (many) + aner/andros (man), and specifically denotes a woman having multiple husbands — practised among some communities in parts of Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand. Polygamy is the most common wrong choice because it is the general umbrella term covering any multi-spouse arrangement, whereas polyandry and polygyny are the gender-specific sub-terms examiners test.
